purpose: High-bandwidth-memory datacenter and unusual AI platforms that remain relevant to local/workstation experimentation, secondary-market monitoring, or architecture comparison.
notes: Manufacturer specifications are authoritative for hardware fields. Marketplace prices are point-in-time observations and not fair-market valuations.
Vendor TOPS/TFLOPS figures are precision- and sparsity-dependent and must not be compared without matching datatypes and assumptions.

Server accelerators often require directed chassis airflow, server-class power delivery, platform firmware support, or proprietary carrier/socket infrastructure; these constraints materially affect local deployment practicality.
Unsupported or deprecated software status is recorded explicitly and must not be inferred from historical product support pages.

hardware.interconnect: third-generation NVLink up to 200 GB/s between a supported adjacent pair
hardware.quantization_compatibility: Strong CUDA support for FP16/BF16/TF32 and Tensor Core INT8/INT4 paths; practical GGUF/AWQ/GPTQ support depends on runtime/kernel selection.
hardware.llm_fit: 24GB VRAM is practical for many 7B-14B models at high precision and a broad set of roughly 20B-32B low-bit models, with room varying substantially by context/KV cache. 933GB/s HBM2 bandwidth is unusually high for a 165W 24GB accelerator and can make decode bandwidth attractive compared with many workstation cards.

pricing.note: Representative A30 24GB used listing observed at CA$3,468.91 plus shipping. This is an asking-price observation and appears poor value versus many newer 24-32GB cards; market prices vary widely.

hardware.interconnect: 2x Infinity Fabric links; up to 92 GB/s peak link bandwidth
hardware.cooling: passive; strong server-style directed airflow required
hardware.software_lifecycle: AMD's current ROCm Compute Profiler compatibility documentation marks MI50/MI60 Vega20 as unsupported. Historical ROCm/HIP software may still be usable with older stacks, but current prebuilt ROCm libraries/tooling must not be assumed to support gfx906 MI60.
hardware.quantization_compatibility: Potentially usable for GGUF/low-bit inference through compatible legacy ROCm/HIP or community paths, but modern prebuilt ROCm support is not verified; treat software setup as experimental.
hardware.llm_fit: 32GB capacity plus 1TB/s HBM2 bandwidth is attractive on paper for 20B-32B low-bit models and split larger models, but software lifecycle, 300W board power and passive cooling dominate practical value.

pricing.note: Used MI60 32GB listing last updated February 19, 2026 showed about CA$701 and was out of stock. Retained as a market reference, not a current buy recommendation.

hardware.quantization_compatibility: Vendor stack supports FP8 and common framework/model-reference workflows; broad consumer-style GGUF compatibility should not be assumed and depends on dedicated Gaudi runtime support.
hardware.llm_fit: 128GB HBM2E and 3.7TB/s bandwidth are highly attractive for very large models and high-throughput inference, but 600W board power, server cooling and software specialization make this a datacenter/advanced-lab platform rather than a normal local-PC accelerator.

pricing.note: No defensible standalone public retail price captured in this pass; Gaudi 3 PCIe is primarily sold through server/OEM channels.

hardware.form_factor: SH5 socket APU; not a conventional PCIe add-in card
hardware.host_interface: PCIe 5.0 x16 plus 8 Infinity Fabric links
hardware.cooling: platform-dependent passive or active server/HPC cooling
hardware.quantization_compatibility: ROCm supports standard AI datatypes and model runtimes on MI300-class hardware; low-bit LLM support depends on runtime kernels and should be benchmarked by exact model/engine.
hardware.llm_fit: Architecturally exceptional for large-model experimentation because CPU and GPU share 128GB of very high-bandwidth HBM3. However, SH5 socket/platform requirements and 550-760W power make it an HPC node architecture, not a drop-in local-workstation option.

pricing.note: MI300A is sold as part of HPC/OEM platforms rather than as a normal retail add-in card; no defensible standalone retail price captured.
